# Edge

```{r}
#| include: false
source("../R/setup.R")
```

Which things in your table are connected to which? `edge` draws one stroke per
row of the table, between the two things named in that row. Every other mark
that draws a stroke is placed by its values on the axes. A `line` and a `path`
join points at their `x` and `y` values, and an `interval` spans two values on
one axis. An `edge` is different: each row gives it only two names, and no
column says where a name is placed on the page. A plot of edges is a **network
diagram**.

So an edge takes no `x`, `y` or `z`. It is the only mark that takes none of the
three. An edge's endpoints come from a [`layout`](../network.qmd), a transform
that reads the two columns of names and places each distinct name once. Write
the *from* column first and the *to* column second, so the sentence states the
direction of each relation. If you swap the two columns, the picture does not
change. It changes
only when you add arrowheads: `style(arrow = "end")` points each edge from the
first column to the second ([What you can set](#what-you-can-set)).

## The network diagram {#the-network-diagram}

A network diagram needs a table with one row per relation. In
`trade_partners`, each row names an exporter and an importer, gives the value of
the goods in rounded billions of dollars, and names the exporter's continent:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(trade_partners)
```

Name the table, then write three things: the mark, the `layout` that derives
it, and the space `network()`:

```{r}
data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(exporter, importer) + network()
```

*"Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, in
the network."*

The 15 countries get 15 positions on the panel, and gog draws one stroke for
each of the 22 rows. Five pairs of countries trade in both directions, and each
pair's two strokes lie on one line. So you can count only 17 lines, and those
five look slightly darker than the rest. No country is labeled: the layout
placed the countries, but no layer draws their names.

An `edge` draws in two spaces only, `network()` and `space()`. A layout computes its positions from
the **graph**. Here a graph is not a chart: it is a set of things and the
relations between them. Each thing is a **node**, and each row is one relation
between two nodes. A node is one name, however many rows it appears in: Germany
is one node in seven rows. A layout counts each row as one step between its two
nodes. Two countries that trade are one step apart, so they are placed close
together, and nodes with more steps between them are placed farther apart. No
column holds a node's position, and turning or flipping the picture changes no
distance, so a position on its own means nothing. In every other space, a
position means something: a value on an axis, a place on the earth, or a share
of a whole, so gog refuses an edge there. In the cube that `space()` draws, the
box around the network carries no numbers, so a position is not read as a value
there either.

A `layout` is not for edges alone. It gives every node one position. It also
writes two columns. `name` holds each node's name, and `degree` holds the number
of rows the node appears in. Two other marks read a layout and draw at those
same positions:

| Mark derived by `layout` | Shape |
|---|---|
| `point * layout` | one dot per node |
| `text * layout + label(name)` | each node's name |
| `edge * layout` | one stroke per relation, the plot above |

The first plot names no country. The plot below draws all three marks, and it
uses both columns the layout writes. `size(degree)` draws a node's dot larger
when the node appears in more rows. `label(name)` draws each node's name, and
[`repel`](text.qmd#repel-moving-labels-off-each-other) moves each name off the
dots and off the other names:

```{r}
data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(exporter, importer) +
  point * layout(exporter, importer) + size(degree) +
  text * layout(exporter, importer) * repel + label(name) +
  network() +
  title("Each node, sized by its degree")
```

*"Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, and
also points derived by layout from exporter to importer, sized by degree, and
also text derived by layout from exporter to importer and repel, label by name,
in the network."*

China appears in nine rows, the United States in eight and Germany in seven. No
other country appears in more than three, so these three have the largest dots.
A pair that trades both ways is two rows but one line, so only seven lines end
at China's dot.

Each layer computes the layout for itself. A layout uses no random numbers, so
the same two columns always give the same positions in the plane. That is why
every dot is exactly where its strokes end. The Network chapter draws this plot
again, in [The nodes and their names](../network.qmd#the-nodes-and-their-names).

The next section draws each stroke with an opacity, a width, a color or a stroke
pattern from its own row.

## Opacity, width, color and pattern, one per row {#opacity-width-color-and-pattern-one-per-row}

In the plots above, every stroke is drawn the same way, so a relation worth 500
billion dollars looks like one worth 50 billion. Each edge is drawn from one
row, so it can take its opacity, its width, its color and its stroke pattern
from that row's values. On an edge, `size` is the width of the stroke. `opacity`
and `size` show a continuous column such as `billions`, the value of each
relation, and the first plot maps it to `opacity`. A faint stroke's ends are hard to find, so
the plot keeps the `point * layout(exporter, importer)` layer, which draws a dot
at each node:

```{r}
data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(exporter, importer) + opacity(billions) +
  point * layout(exporter, importer) +
  network() +
  title("More trade, darker stroke")
```

*"Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer,
opacity by billions, and also points derived by layout from exporter to
importer, in the network."*

The three darkest strokes meet at one node. This plot draws no names, but every
node is at the same position as in the plot with names, in [The network
diagram](#the-network-diagram). So the node where they meet is the United
States. China, Mexico and Canada each export more than 400 billion dollars of
goods to it.

The width of a stroke can come from its row in the same way. `size(billions)`
draws a stroke wider where the relation is worth more:

```{r}
data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(exporter, importer) + size(billions) +
  point * layout(exporter, importer) +
  network() +
  title("More trade, wider stroke")
```

*"Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer,
sized by billions, and also points derived by layout from exporter to importer,
in the network."*

The three widest strokes are the three darkest in the plot above, and they meet
at the United States. The legend draws a line at three values: 50, 275 and 500
billion dollars. Width also keeps the smallest relations in view: France to
Spain, worth 50 billion, is a thin stroke here, and nearly disappears in the
opacity plot.

On `line`, `size` and `opacity` are only settings: gog keeps one width and one
opacity for a whole line ([Stroke width and
opacity](line.qmd#stroke-width-and-opacity)). An edge draws one stroke per row,
so each row gives its stroke a width and an opacity of its own.

Which exports come from each continent? On an edge, `color` needs a categorical
column. The `continent` column holds the continent of each row's exporter, and
it has four values. A continuous column such as `billions` is refused there; map
it to `opacity` or `size`, as above. The names are written in this plot, so you
can see which two countries each stroke joins:

```{r}
data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(exporter, importer) + color(continent) +
  point * layout(exporter, importer) +
  text * layout(exporter, importer) * repel + label(name) +
  network() +
  title("Each stroke, colored by its exporter's continent")
```

*"Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, colored
by continent, and also points derived by layout from exporter to importer, and
also text derived by layout from exporter to importer and repel, label by name,
in the network."*

Europe's strokes all touch Germany, except France's stroke to Spain. The
Americas' strokes all touch the United States, except Brazil's stroke to China.
Oceania has one stroke, from Australia to China.

`color(exporter)` draws as well, with one color for each of the twelve
exporters. Twelve colors are hard to distinguish on a stroke a pixel or two
wide. Mexico, Canada and the Netherlands also get a color in the legend and on
no stroke, because each trades with one partner only, and the partner's row is
drawn over theirs. With `continent`, four colors are easy to distinguish, and
every color in the legend is on a stroke.

Strokes are drawn in row order, so where two countries trade both ways, the
later row's stroke covers the other. Between China and Germany, Germany's row
comes later, and the stroke shows mostly Europe's color.

The stroke pattern can come from a column too. `pattern(continent)` gives each
continent a stroke pattern, the way `color(continent)` gave each a color above:

```{r}
data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(exporter, importer) + pattern(continent) +
  point * layout(exporter, importer) +
  text * layout(exporter, importer) * repel + label(name) +
  network() +
  title("Each stroke, patterned by its exporter's continent")
```

*"Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer,
patterned by continent, and also points derived by layout from exporter to
importer, and also text derived by layout from exporter to importer and repel,
label by name, in the network."*

The stroke patterns follow the order in which the continents first appear in
the `continent` column: Asia's strokes are solid, the Americas' are dashed,
Europe's are dotted and Oceania's are dotdash. Between China and Germany,
Germany's dotted stroke is drawn over China's solid one, and the solid stroke
shows through the gaps, so the line looks solid.

There are five stroke patterns: solid, dashed, dotted, dotdash and longdash. A
column with more than five categories repeats them from the start.

## Transforms it takes {#transforms-it-takes}

A transform computes new values from the rows, and the mark draws those values
instead of the rows. The table lists, by kind, the transforms an edge takes and
the ones it refuses:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
mark_transforms("edge")
```

An edge takes one transform, `layout`. It is marked ●: gog cannot draw an edge
without it, because without a layout an edge has no ends. The plots below show
it twice: in the plane, and in a cube.

**Layouts.** `layout` places each node once, and an edge draws one stroke
between the two nodes of each row. It needs `network()` or `space()`, where no
axis carries numbers, because a node's position is not a value on any axis.
`network()` places the nodes in the plane, as every plot above does. Write
`space()` in its place, here with a viewing angle, `space(turn = 35, tilt =
20)`, and the layout places them in a cube instead.
Both numbers are degrees, and [The viewing
angle](../space.qmd#the-viewing-angle) explains them. A `point`
layer draws a dot at each node, so the ends of each stroke are easy to find:

```{r}
((data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(exporter, importer) +
    point * layout(exporter, importer) + network() + title("edge * layout")) |
   (data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(exporter, importer) +
      point * layout(exporter, importer) + space(turn = 35, tilt = 20) +
      title("edge * layout, in a cube"))) +
  theme(height = 420)
```

*"Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, and
also points derived by layout from exporter to importer, in the network, beside
the same in the cube, turned 35, tilted 20."*

The cube holds the same 22 strokes. Every node takes a new position in the
cube, because the layout places the nodes in three directions instead of two.
The Network chapter names each node in the cube, in [The network in the
cube](../network.qmd#the-network-in-the-cube), and shows how to turn it with a
drag in the web edition.

An edge refuses every transform in the Refuses column above. Most of them
compute a value to place on an axis, or move a mark along one, and an edge has
no axis. The other three, in the same row of the table as `layout`, compute
shapes for different marks: `partition`
gives rectangles to a [`zone`](zone.qmd), `flow` gives bands to a
[`ribbon`](ribbon.qmd), and `cluster` gives branches to a [`path`](path.qmd).

## What you can set {#what-you-can-set}

Some choices come from no column: how thick every stroke is, or one stroke pattern
for all of them. You set those in the sentence, with `style()`, and each mark takes
its own settings. [Setting vs mapping](../style.qmd) shows how a setting differs from mapping a
column. These are an edge's settings, with the values each accepts:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
mark_options("edge")
```

`style(size = )`, `style(color = )`, `style(opacity = )` and
`style(pattern = )` give every stroke the same value. A mapping such as
`size(billions)` gives each stroke its own. The settings table above lists every stroke pattern that `style(pattern = )` accepts.

One layer cannot both map a channel and set it. gog refuses this sentence, which
maps `continent` to `color` and also sets the color to red:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(exporter, importer) + color(continent) +
  style(color = "red") + network()
```

The message names two fixes: keep `color(continent)` to show the data, or
`style(color = "red")` to give every edge one color.

`style(arrow = )` draws an arrowhead on each stroke. With `"end"`, it is at the
node in the second column of `layout()`, the *to* column. With `"start"`, it is
at the node in the first column, and with `"both"`, at both nodes. Each
arrowhead ends outside the dot that a `point * layout` layer draws at the node,
so the dot does not cover it:

```{r}
data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(exporter, importer) + style(arrow = "end") +
  point * layout(exporter, importer) +
  network() +
  title("Each stroke points at its importer")
```

*"Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, with
arrow end, and also points derived by layout from exporter to importer, in the
network."*

The [grid of every mark and every setting](../style.qmd#what-you-can-set) shows
which other marks share this list. What a mark *maps* rather than sets is its
row on the [grid of marks and channels](../combinations.qmd#marks-and-channels).

## What it refuses {#what-it-refuses}

The other marks take their positions from `x` and `y`, so you may try binding
`x` and `y` to an edge. Only a `layout` places an edge's two ends. With `x` and
`y` and no layout, the edge has nothing to draw, so gog refuses the sentence:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(trade_partners) + edge + x(billions) + y(exporter)
```

The message shows what to write instead: name the two endpoint columns in
`layout()` and draw it in `network()`.

A `layout` computes its positions from the graph, and no column holds them, so
an axis has no value to show for them. Without `network()`, a sentence is in the
plane, and the plane has axes. So gog refuses this sentence, which leaves
`network()` out:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(exporter, importer)
```

The message gives two ways to draw it: flat with `+ network()`, or in the cube
with `+ space(turn = 30, tilt = 25)`.

The [Network](../network.qmd) chapter shows four more refusals: a mark other than `edge`, `point` or `text`
with `* layout`, an
`x()` in a sentence with a layout, `network()` with no layout, and a row from a
node to itself. It explains why a brush is refused there too.

## What comes next {#what-comes-next}

An edge never has an axis, because a layout places both of its endpoints. Most
other marks are placed by their values on the axes. [Scales](../scales.qmd)
shows how a value becomes a position on an axis.
